name: orbital-trap-frequency
description: An electrostatic orbital trap, measured by the one thing it measures: the frequency of the ion's axial oscillation. The field is quadro-logarithmic and analytic, which is the exact statement of the geometry rather than an approximation to it - the electrode shapes that produce this field ARE its own equipotentials. omega = sqrt(q k / m) carries no radius, no angular momentum and no amplitude, so the frequency is the same for every ion of a given mass to charge whatever orbit it is on. Mass is read from a frequency only because of that independence, and the expectation here is that closed form with k and m/z declared: 312.666 kHz for m/z 500 at 20 V/mm^2. The ion is launched off the axis AND off the centre plane, which is what an injection does: it arrives through a slot at a radius inside the characteristic one, tangentially, and the axial offset is what starts the oscillation. Over the 160 oscillations followed here it returns to its launch radius and its launch axial offset, which is the isochronism the instrument rests on. The measured frequency is Fourier-limited rather than exact, and that is physically right rather than a shortcoming: the uncertainty is one over the record length, which is the same relation that makes a real analyser's resolving power grow with the length of its transient. At 40 oscillations the error is 4.6e-3, at 160 it is 5.8e-4, at 640 it is 3.7e-4.

curvature.description: Axial curvature of the potential, conventionally k. The one number the measured frequency comes from: omega = sqrt(q k / m), and nothing else enters it. At 20 V/mm^2 an m/z 500 ion oscillates at 313 kHz and is injected through 1.5 keV, which is the scale a compact orbital analyser runs at.

characteristicRadius.description: The radius at which the radial field vanishes, conventionally Rm. Inside it an ion is pulled toward the spindle and can orbit; outside it is pushed away, which is why a real trap has its outer electrode there.

orbitRadius.description: Where the ion is injected, between the spindle and the characteristic radius. It changes the orbit and the tangential speed needed to hold it - and does not change the axial frequency at all, which is the property the device rests on.

axialOffset.description: How far off the centre plane the ion enters. This is the amplitude of the axial oscillation, and it does not change its frequency: a harmonic well is isochronous, which is why a packet spread along the axis still gives one line.

massToCharge.description: The quantity being measured. The axial frequency goes as its inverse square root, which is the calibration law of every orbital analyser.

turns.description: How many axial oscillations to follow. A real transient is hundreds of thousands, since the resolving power grows with the length of the record; this is enough to measure a frequency.

orbitPotential.description: The circular-orbit condition written as the accelerating potential whose speed it is: m v^2 / 2q, which is k (Rm^2 - r^2) / 4. Independent of mass to charge, which is why one injection energy serves every ion an orbital analyser accepts.

axialPeriod.description: The axial period at this working point. Written as the reference times a dimensionless ratio, because sqrt is dimensionless-only - the square root of a mass over a curvature has no representation in an integer-exponent dimension system, and the grammar refuses it rather than dropping the dimension.

flightTime.description: Long enough for the declared number of axial oscillations.

referenceMass.description: The mass the reference period below was measured at. Only the ratio to massToCharge is used, so this is a unit-bearing constant rather than a knob.

referenceCurvature.description: The curvature the reference period was measured at, likewise. Changing either reference without the other changes nothing, since they appear only as ratios.

referencePeriod.description: The axial period at the reference mass and curvature. This is the one number here the grammar cannot derive: the period is 2 pi sqrt(m / (q k)) and the grammar has no elementary charge, so a dimensionless ratio has to be anchored to a measured one. Everything else scales off it exactly.
